title: Churches around the world
hook: from Ethiopian round churches to Korean hilltop crosses

segments.voice: Yesterday, choirs: four odd notes that turn into one chord. Your line was many voices. Where did you hear people making one sound together? Day one thousand three hundred sixty-seven.

On a green Ethiopian hillside, a church stands in a ring of old trees. Its walls make a circle, and its roof rises to a point. People in white shawls stand outside the doors and pray toward the center. Now cross the world to a Korean city after dark. From a high window, you can see red crosses glowing on rooftops all over the hills, like a field of small lit signs. Same faith, two very different buildings. Neither one looks like the white steeple some people picture when they hear the word church. Today: churches around the world.
screen: `A ROUND CHURCH IN A RING OF TREES.`

segments.voice: Start with a promise in the book of Acts. Before Jesus is taken up, he tells his friends: "ye shall be witnesses unto me both in Jerusalem, and in all Judaea, and in Samaria, and unto the uttermost part of the earth." The story moves outward from one city. A few chapters later, Acts shows it leaving the map. An official from Ethiopia, riding home in his chariot, reading the prophet Isaiah, meets Philip on a desert road. They pass water, and the man says: "See, here is water; what doth hinder me to be baptized?" Next, the round church. In the Ethiopian Orthodox Church, some churches are built in a circle, rings within rings, with the most holy place at the very center, where only priests go. The building is a map of drawing near to God: outer ring, inner ring, heart. In Lalibela, tradition says, churches were carved straight down into solid rock. Then the lit crosses. In Korea, crosses glowing red or white at night mark churches across the cities, so that the skyline itself announces them. A church there might be a single floor above a shop. The shape is new. The prayer inside is the same old prayer. Last, a conversation at a well. A Samaritan woman asks Jesus which mountain is the right place to worship. He answers: "the hour cometh, when ye shall neither in this mountain, nor yet at Jerusalem, worship the Father." No one mountain. No one shape. That's why a church in the rock, a church in a ring of trees and a church above a shop can all be called by the same name.
screen: `TO THE UTTERMOST PART OF THE EARTH.`
`A ROUND CHURCH, THE HOLY PLACE AT ITS HEART.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look at a church from another continent. If you can, find a photo of one far from where you live: a round church in Ethiopia, a wooden church in the far north, a church in a Korean city. Settle, and breathe. Look slowly. Where are the doors? Where does the light come in? What's at the center? Then imagine the people who'll walk in this week, and what they'll carry with them. If you pray, you can pray for that congregation. If you don't, simply hold them in mind for a moment. The bell holds the time.
Churches around the world. Round, carved, domed, lit up at night: the many shapes the same faith takes in different places.

Your line: many shapes. Today, notice one building you pass that's used for prayer, any kind, and look at its shape for a moment, as if you'd flown across the world to see it. Day one thousand three hundred sixty-seven.

howItsDone: Christians around the world worship in buildings of many shapes: round churches and rock-hewn churches in Ethiopia, domed churches in the Orthodox world, Gothic cathedrals, white wooden chapels, and churches above shops in Korean cities marked by lit crosses.

original.note: Greek: assembly. the New Testament's word for church names people, as in "the church that is in their house."

trapdoor: what you thought: a church looks like a white steeple on a hill.
what it means: the same faith takes many shapes: round, carved in rock, lit up at night, upstairs from a shop.
what a scholar hears: ekklesia, an assembly. Paul greets "the church that is in their house": here the word names people, not a building.
